Coordination

Wedding coordinators across Australia

A wedding coordinator does not plan your wedding. They take the plan you have already built, confirm every supplier, write the run sheet and manage the day, so nobody is ringing the couple about the chairs.

Find a wedding coordinatorPlanner vs coordinator
  • Handover four to six weeks out
  • Your suppliers stay exactly as booked
  • Free to enquire

What does a wedding coordinator do?

A wedding coordinator takes ownership of a finished plan and runs it. The handover normally happens four to six weeks before the wedding, at which point the coordinator reads everything you have built, contacts every supplier to confirm times and access, writes a single run sheet that all of them work from, and then manages the day itself from bump in to bump out.

The reason this role exists is simple. Planning a wedding and hosting one are different jobs, and the second one is impossible to do while you are also the person the florist rings at 8am. A coordinator becomes that contact. Wedding coordination services are the most commonly bought planning product in Australia for exactly that reason: they are the smallest amount of help that solves the biggest problem.

The confusion

Venue coordinator, or one of your own?

This is the single most common misunderstanding in Australian wedding planning, and it costs couples real money when they get it wrong.

Where the two roles differ. Venue coordinator inclusions vary by venue, so confirm yours in writing.
Venue coordinatorYour own coordinator
Works forThe venueYou
Usually costsIncluded in the venue feeBooked and paid separately
Covers your suppliersOnly the ones inside the venue contractAll of them, wherever they come from
Writes your run sheetThe venue's timings, not your whole dayYes, and circulates it to every supplier
On site forThe venue's operating hoursBump in through to pack down
Handles the ceremonyOnly if it is at the venueYes, including travel between sites
Is there when a supplier failsManages venue staffManages the problem

Scroll the table sideways to see every column.

Both roles are useful and they are not alternatives. A venue coordinator makes the venue run properly. Your own coordinator makes your wedding run properly, including the two thirds of it that has nothing to do with the venue.

The handover

What happens in the four to six weeks before

01

Handover meeting

You give the coordinator everything: contracts, contacts, floor plans, timings, the seating chart and the parts you are worried about.

02

Supplier confirmation

The coordinator contacts every supplier, confirms arrival times, access, power, meals and pack down, and finds the gaps you did not know were there.

03

Run sheet built and circulated

One document, one version, sent to every supplier and to the venue. This is the deliverable that actually protects the day.

04

The day itself

The coordinator is first on site and last off it, and is the contact for every supplier, so you are not.

Two sites

When the ceremony and the reception are in different places

A two-site wedding day is the single most common thing that turns a straightforward coordination job into a complicated one, and it is worth raising in the first conversation.

With one site, the coordinator arrives, sets up, runs the day and packs down in one place. With two, almost everything doubles. There are two bump ins, often two styling installs, two sets of access rules, and a travel window in the middle that has to hold even if the ceremony runs late. Some suppliers charge a second delivery. Some items get moved between sites by someone, and that someone needs naming in the run sheet.

The guest transfer is the part most couples underestimate. Moving 90 people between a ceremony and a reception takes far longer than the drive does, because the last car does not leave when the first one does. A coordinator will usually build in more buffer than you think is necessary, and they are almost always right.

If your day has two sites, ask whether the quote includes a second coordinator. On a guest count above roughly 80, one person cannot be packing down a ceremony and receiving suppliers at a reception at the same time.

Ask these three about a two-site day

Who moves the items between sites, what time does the call get made if the ceremony runs late, and is a second coordinator included or quoted separately.

Limits

What a coordinator cannot fix

Coordination solves a specific problem very well. Being honest about what it does not solve saves an uncomfortable conversation at week two of the handover.

A plan with holes in it

If suppliers are still unbooked at handover, a coordinator is not quoted to source them. They will tell you what is missing and may help where they can, but filling gaps is planning work and it changes the scope.

Look at partial planning

A budget that has already blown out

A coordinator arriving four to six weeks out cannot renegotiate contracts that were signed in month three. Budget control is a planning job and it has to start early to work.

A decision nobody has made

Seating, speech order, the wet weather call. A coordinator will push you to settle these and will set a deadline for each, but they cannot make them for you.

A venue restriction you agreed to

Noise curfews, bump out times and supplier restrictions sit in your venue contract. A coordinator works within them and will find out what they actually are, which is often the first time anyone has read them properly.

Cost

What wedding coordination costs in Australia

Published Australian figures put a day-of coordinator at roughly $1,500 to $2,000 according to Easy Weddings, in a guide updated in February 2026, and at $1,000 to $5,000 according to Airtasker's Australian cost guide updated in February 2025. The spread reflects how much is included before the day, not how many hours are worked on it.

Three things move the price. The first is how early the handover starts, because a six week handover involves far more supplier work than a two week one. The second is whether the ceremony and reception are at the same site, since two sites means travel, a second bump in and often a second staff member. The third is guest count, which drives how many people the coordinator needs on the ground.

Compare quotes on the handover length and the on-site hours rather than on the headline figure. A cheaper quote with a two week handover and eight hours on site is not the same product as a dearer one with six weeks and full-day cover.

Straight answers

Questions about wedding coordination

What is the difference between a wedding planner and a wedding coordinator?

A wedding planner builds the plan with you over months: concept, venue, suppliers, budget and timeline. A coordinator takes a finished plan four to six weeks out, confirms it and runs the day. Planners are engaged early, coordinators late. Our comparison guide sets out the full difference.

Do I still need a wedding coordinator if my venue has one?

Many couples book both. A venue coordinator works for the venue and manages what happens inside it. Your own coordinator works for you and manages the whole day, including the suppliers who are not part of the venue contract and the ceremony if it is somewhere else.

How much does a day of coordinator cost?

Easy Weddings, updated February 2026, puts a day-of coordinator at roughly $1,500 to $2,000. Airtasker's Australian guide gives $1,000 to $5,000. The difference is mostly the length of the handover period and whether the ceremony and reception are at the same site.

When should you book one?

Two to three months before the wedding is the usual window, which allows the handover to start four to six weeks out. Some coordinators will decline a booking inside six weeks because they cannot do the supplier confirmation work properly in the time available.

What do I need to give a coordinator at handover?

Every supplier contract and contact, the venue floor plan, your timings, the seating chart, any access or bump in restrictions, and an honest list of what you are worried about. The last one is the most useful and the one people leave out.
